source.title: Is there "Secret Sauce'' in Large Language Model Development?
source.authors: Matthias Mertens; Natalia Fischl-Lanzoni; Neil Thompson

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some figure text is garbled, but the relevant regression results are stated in text or tables.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses observational regressions of downstream benchmark scores on training compute, rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss or running controlled pretraining scaling experiments.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own compute–benchmark regressions and robustness analyses. It cites prior loss scaling laws and downstream scaling work, but cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits its own observational regressions of logit downstream benchmark scores on log training compute across 809 released LLMs (785 for MATH Level 5). These bear directly on V6. It does not measure pretraining loss, extrapolation, allocation, shape or other modalities. Its robustness checks probe its own decomposition, not the fit-dependence of published scaling laws, so they do not test V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that training compute drives 80–90% of frontier MMLU-Pro performance. Developer-specific 'secret sauce' explains 14–18% of variation, and shared progress gives about 7.5x effective compute. These efficiency factors, plus large within-developer variation, matter most below the frontier. MATH Level 5 results are qualitatively similar.
record.recipe_differences: Uses observational data from released models and downstream benchmark scores with logit regression and fixed effects, rather than controlled pretraining runs measuring held-out cross-entropy loss or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report similar findings under logistic transformations with shape parameters v = 0.7 and v = 1.2, and under alternative time-effect specifications. Period-by-compute interactions are not statistically significant.

fits_no_version.finding: The compute slope on logit MMLU-Pro does not change significantly across three release periods (interactions 0.128 and 0.160, both not significant).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The downstream compute–performance elasticity is stable over successive model generations; algorithmic progress acts as a multiplicative compute shift rather than changing the exponent.

fits_no_version.finding: Shared algorithmic progress gives a 7.5x effective-compute gain over the window, and the estimate is robust to link function (7.07x, 7.76x).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Algorithmic progress shifts downstream scaling curves by a measurable effective-compute factor over time.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says the dataset and program files are published under a link, but no URL is present in the supplied text.
record.problems: The study is observational and does not directly measure held-out pretraining loss or validate small-run extrapolations. It focuses on non-reasoning models and a limited set of benchmarks. The authors note substantial uncertainty in some proprietary-model parameter and token estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported compute–performance regression result was omitted.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute is not measured.
No small-run fit is extrapolated to larger runs.
There is no fixed-compute allocation analysis.
No other modalities or training regimes are studied.
Only MMLU-Pro and MATH Level 5 are covered, both with in-sample observational fits. There is no out-of-sample prediction of larger models' scores, and reasoning models are excluded.
Parameter counting, schedule, data and fitting-method effects on loss-law exponents are not tested. Neither is Kaplan–Hoffmann disagreement or bending of loss curves.

missing.what: Shapley decomposition: scaling explains 32% of MMLU-Pro variance in the full sample, 45% among major developers, and 44.3% for MATH Level 5. Model residuals explain 32–47%.
Frontier decomposition: scaling accounts for 77% to 88% of performance, with +2.9 of +2.5 log-odds from Llama2 70B to GPT-4.5.
Excluding LifeArchitect estimates gives a compute coefficient of 0.80*** (SE 0.21) on 793 LLMs.
Compute coefficients by subsample: 0.885 for major developers, 1.096 below median FLOPs, 0.467 above median FLOPs.
Model-specific efficiency spread: 41x (90–10 gap) for MMLU-Pro and 186x for MATH Level 5.

record.verdict_notes: Observational, in-sample fits on released models with estimated compute; some proprietary parameter and token counts are uncertain. The compute coefficient is not comparable across link transformations. The reader's V7 'challenges' label is removed: robustness of the study's own decomposition is not evidence about the fit-dependence of published scaling laws.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict the loss of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is studied.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or training regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer are tested as scaling-law settings.
The analysis tests observational association with MMLU-Pro and MATH Level 5 scores, not broad downstream-task coverage or out-of-sample prediction.

The study checks selected link-function and time-effect specifications and whether compute elasticity changes across its three periods. It does not test parameter-counting choices, training schedules, data choices, compute-optimal allocation, disagreement between Kaplan and Hoffmann, or whether pretraining-loss curves bend.

rows.check: This is the study's own robustness check on the shared-progress compute factor under an alternative link function. It is not a measure of how scaling-law exponents or the compute-optimal split depend on fitting choices, so it does not bear on V7. The compute coefficient itself is not comparable across link scales (1.45 vs 0.79).

relationships.condition: Observational cross-developer samples of non-reasoning LLMs, MMLU-Pro (809) and MATH Level 5 (785)
relationships.reason: Logit benchmark score rises significantly with log compute (0.79*** and 0.92***). The authors report that the logistic form fits the raw data well (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: Logit scores increased significantly with log compute, with coefficients 0.79 for MMLU-Pro and 0.92 for MATH Level 5, and logistic curves fitted the data well.

relationships.condition: Across developers and individual models at given compute
relationships.reason: Per the text (no row): compute explains only about 32% of MMLU-Pro variance. Developer and model effects shift effective compute by up to 61x and 41x (90–10 gap), so compute alone predicts scores only loosely. The R2 values in R1 and R2 are about 0.53.
relationships.display_finding: Compute explained about 32% of MMLU-Pro variance, while developer and model effects shifted effective compute by up to 61-fold and 41-fold across the 90th-to-10th percentile gap, with other reported fits near R²=0.53.

relation.reason: The study estimates its own compute–performance relationships and decomposes variation relevant to downstream predictability.

tranche.reason: Observational regressions of downstream benchmark performance on training compute test V6 using a different method and measure from controlled pretraining-loss scaling experiments.

source_check.notes: Results concern observational associations in non-reasoning models, not causal effects or validated out-of-sample extrapolation. The 32% scaling contribution and full-model R2 describe different quantities.

statements.correction: MMLU-Pro: scaling Shapley contribution=32%; full regression R2=0.526; log-compute coefficient=0.789***; developer and model residual effects substantial; V6 label=limits_scope for prediction from compute alone.
statements.problem: The 32% figure is supported, but it is a Shapley contribution rather than a reported compute-only regression R2. This study qualifies compute-only predictability; its significant positive associations do not establish an absent or reversed scaling effect warranting challenges.
